Why it keeps hurting

Your knee should not have to manage the whole movement by itself.

Walking, running, squatting, and climbing stairs should spread effort through your whole body. When the foot and ankle, hip and pelvis, or trunk contribute less, the knee works in isolation. One pattern Garrett often sees is the knee doing too much for too long.

01

Why the knee starts working alone

The foot and ankle help receive the ground. The hip and pelvis help organize the leg. The trunk helps carry force across the body. When one or more of those regions contribute less, the knee has to manage motion and stability with less support.

02

Why stronger quads may not solve it

Stronger quads can be useful, but strength at the knee does not automatically reconnect the rest of the body. If the movement still begins and ends at the knee, adding load can ask the same isolated pattern to work harder.

03

Why relief may not change the pattern

A brace can change how force reaches the knee, and an injection can reduce symptoms for some people. Neither automatically changes how the rest of the body shares the movement. Garrett looks for the missing contribution, then guides a setup that lets it participate again.

The goal is not to make the knee do a better job alone. Once the foot and ankle, hip and pelvis, and trunk share the movement again, the knee can stop working so hard by itself.

FAQ

Common questions.

If something isn't here, ask on a free discovery call. Garrett answers everything before you book a paid session.

My MRI shows nothing wrong with my knee. Why does it still hurt?

+

An MRI can help identify certain structural issues, but imaging and pain do not always line up. A knee can still hurt when it is doing too much of a movement by itself. Garrett looks at how the whole body is sharing the work. This does not replace medical evaluation.

What is runner's knee and can it be treated without stopping running?

+

Runner's knee, or patellofemoral pain, is pain around or behind the kneecap. It can have several contributors. In Garrett's work, a common pattern is the knee working in isolation while the foot and ankle, hip and pelvis, and trunk contribute less. Whether to keep running depends on your symptoms and medical guidance. The goal is to restore more shared movement, not push through pain.

I have IT band syndrome. Does foam rolling help?

+

Foam rolling can change how the area feels for a while. It does not show why the outside of the leg keeps taking on so much work. Garrett looks at how the foot and ankle, knee, hip and pelvis, and trunk participate together, then guides the parts that are contributing less back into the movement.

I was told I need a knee replacement. Is it worth trying this first?

+

A recommendation for knee replacement is a medical decision. Amari does not replace that evaluation or claim to reverse arthritis. If your clinician says guided movement is appropriate, Garrett can help explore whether the rest of your body can share more of the work, which may change how the knee feels and functions.

I sit at a desk all day. Could that be causing my knee pain?

+

Sitting can reduce the movement options available through the ankles, hips, pelvis, and trunk, but it is rarely the only factor. When you stand up, the knee may end up doing more because the rest of the body is contributing less. Garrett looks at that whole pattern instead of assuming one muscle or one habit caused the pain.
